items.explanation: The author argues examinations measure a narrow performance yet decide lives, that the system then organises itself around the test, and that coaching makes the test measure coaching rather than ability. Abolition is explicitly rejected.
options: Examinations measure performance narrowly yet carry life-deciding weight, distorting education itself, so their verdict should be treated as a verdict on a performance rather than on a person.
Examinations should be abolished because they are completely unfair.
Interviews and recommendations are fairer than examinations in every respect.
Coaching improves examinations by making them measure ability more accurately.
items.passage: Every year, millions of students sit examinations that will decide where they study, what they earn and how they are regarded for the rest of their lives. The examination presents itself as a neutral instrument, a fair measure of ability that sorts the deserving from the undeserving. The claim is worth examining, because an examination measures something narrower than it pretends to. It measures performance on a particular day, on a particular set of questions, under particular conditions of stress and preparation. A student who falls ill, who cannot afford coaching, or who thinks slowly but deeply will score lower than the examination claims their ability warrants, and the gap between the score and the ability is not a rounding error but the whole story for the student concerned. Defenders reply that no system is perfect, and that examinations, for all their faults, are fairer than the alternatives: interviews that reward confidence, recommendations that reward connections, portfolios that reward wealth. The reply is fair as far as it goes, but it answers the wrong question. The question is not whether examinations are better than interviews but whether a single high-stakes test should carry the weight it does, when its measurement is so narrow and its consequences so large. A test that decides a life in three hours invites the whole education system to organise itself around it. Teachers teach to the test, students learn to the test, and the curriculum narrows to what can be examined quickly. The subjects that cannot be reduced to a timed question, judgement, originality, moral reasoning, disappear from the classroom, not because they are unimportant but because they are untestable. The result is a system that is efficient at sorting and poor at educating, and the irony is that the sorting itself becomes less accurate as the system adapts to it: when everyone is coached to the test, the test stops measuring ability and starts measuring coaching. None of this means examinations should be abolished. A society needs some way to compare students from different schools, and a well-designed examination is better than patronage. The pressure does not fall evenly. A student from a wealthy family can afford coaching, quiet study space and repeated attempts; a student from a poor family cannot, and the examination, which claims to measure ability, ends up measuring resources. The gap is not a flaw in the design of any particular test but a consequence of treating a single performance as a verdict. When the stakes are high enough, those with resources will always find ways to buy an advantage, and the test will measure the advantage rather than the ability it was designed to capture. The fairest examination in the world cannot fix an unfair starting line. But the weight given to a single examination, and the narrowness of what it measures, should make us cautious about treating its verdict as a verdict on a person rather than on a performance.

items.explanation: The passage says a programme that cools the planet would create farmers whose harvests depend on the cooler climate, cities whose heatwaves have eased and governments that have built plans around the new temperature, and that each year of spraying would make stopping harder until the decision to stop becomes a political crisis. The point matters because it shows the programme locks itself in, which is one reason the decision cannot be treated as purely technical.
options: Once spraying begins, farmers, cities and governments build their plans around the cooler climate, so each year of spraying makes stopping harder and the decision to stop becomes a political crisis.
The programme would create jobs for the people who operate the spraying equipment, so employment would rise and the programme would pay for itself.
Countries that benefit from the cooler climate would form a coalition to govern the spraying fairly, solving the governance problem.
The constituency would be the scientists who study the programme, who would demand more research funding each year.
items.passage: The idea is seductive in its simplicity. If the planet is warming because greenhouse gases trap heat, why not reflect a little of the sun's energy back into space? Spraying fine particles into the stratosphere, or brightening the clouds above the oceans, could cool the Earth within months, at a cost far lower than rebuilding the world's energy system. The proposal, known as solar radiation management, has moved from science fiction to serious policy discussion, and its advocates make a powerful case. The climate is changing faster than societies are cutting emissions, and a temporary cooling could buy time, preventing the crossing of thresholds that cannot be uncrossed. The case against it is not that it would fail to cool the planet. It is that cooling the planet is not the same as fixing the climate. Reflecting sunlight does nothing about the carbon dioxide accumulating in the oceans, which is acidifying them and threatening the marine food chains on which a billion people depend. It would also have to be maintained indefinitely: stop the spraying and the suppressed warming returns within years, faster than societies could adapt. Worse, the power to set the planet's temperature would fall to whoever controlled the spraying. A country that cooled the Earth to suit its own harvests might dry the monsoon on which another country depends, and there is no institution on Earth capable of governing such a decision fairly. The deepest objection is moral hazard. A cheap technical fix, even a hypothetical one, gives governments an excuse to postpone the hard work of cutting emissions, and the postponement is itself a decision with consequences. There is also the question of who decides when to stop. A programme that cools the planet would create its own constituency: farmers whose harvests depend on the cooler climate, cities whose heatwaves have eased, governments that have built their plans around the new temperature. Each year of spraying would make stopping harder, and the decision to stop would itself become a political crisis. The programme would also interact with the climate in ways that are hard to predict. Cooling the planet unevenly could shift rainfall patterns, drying some regions while flooding others, and the models that predict these effects disagree about where the rain would fall. A decision taken to help one region could harm another, and the harmed region would have no court to appeal to. These uncertainties do not prove the idea should never be tried, but they show that the decision cannot be treated as a purely technical one, to be settled by comparing temperatures. It is a decision about who bears the risk, and no model can answer that question on its own. The honest conclusion is not that solar radiation management should never be researched. It is that the question cannot be answered by engineers alone, because it is a question about who governs the sky, and no one has yet proposed an answer to that.

items.explanation: Both sides have a point, which is what makes the argument difficult: preservation matters, and some returned objects have been damaged, but preservation is not neutral, and custody without consent is another name for theft. The honest approach is to examine each case on its own facts. The second and third options take one side only, and the fourth states that the honest question is not whether the statue is safer in London or in Lagos.
options: Both sides have a point, and the honest question is who gets to decide, on what grounds, examined case by case rather than by a single rule.
All statues should be returned at once, since custody without consent is theft.
Museums should never discuss return, since preservation is the only thing that matters.
The statue is safer in London than in Lagos, and safety settles the question.
items.passage: A statue that was taken from a temple two hundred years ago now stands in a museum thousands of miles away, admired by visitors who know nothing of the place it came from. The museum argues that it is a custodian, not an owner: it preserves the statue, studies it, and shows it to the world, and returning it would put it at risk. The country of origin argues that custody without consent is another name for theft, and that a statue kept from the community that made it has lost half its meaning. Both sides have a point, which is what makes the argument difficult. Preservation matters, and some objects returned to unstable places have indeed been damaged or lost. But preservation is not a neutral act. To preserve an object in a foreign museum is also to decide whose story it tells, and the story told in the museum is rarely the story the makers would have told. The honest question is not whether the statue is safer in London or in Lagos but who gets to decide, and on what grounds. The argument is complicated by the fact that many objects were not simply stolen but bought, gifted or exchanged under circumstances that are hard to judge from a distance. A statue sold by a local ruler two centuries ago was a transaction, but it was a transaction between parties of vastly unequal power, and the price paid reflected that inequality. The line between a sale and a seizure is not always sharp, and museums have used that ambiguity to resist claims they find inconvenient. The honest approach is to examine each case on its own facts rather than applying a single rule to all of them. Some objects were clearly looted; some were clearly bought fairly; most lie somewhere between, and the negotiation should reflect that complexity rather than pretending it does not exist. A museum that refuses even to discuss return is not preserving heritage; it is asserting ownership, and ownership asserted over a stolen object is a continuation of the taking, not its end.

items.explanation: The strong version, that language determines thought, has few defenders left, and the weaker version, that language influences thought, is harder to dismiss. What the research shows is narrower: language shapes attention, making some distinctions easy to notice and others easy to miss. The snow-words claim rested on shaky counting, and the effects are real but modest, fading when the task changes, which is not the same as having no effect.

items.passage: Do people who speak different languages think differently? The question has divided scholars for a century. The strong version of the claim, that language determines thought, has few defenders left. No one seriously argues that a person cannot think a thought for which their language has no word. The weaker version, that language influences thought, is harder to dismiss. Speakers of languages that mark the future differently save money at different rates, or so one famous study claimed. Speakers of languages with many words for snow were once said to see snow differently, a claim that turned out to rest on shaky counting. The evidence is messy because the question is messy: language, culture and environment move together, and separating their effects is difficult. What the research does show is narrower and more interesting. Language shapes attention: it makes some distinctions easy to notice and others easy to miss. A language that obliges its speakers to mark the direction of an event will make its speakers unusually good at keeping track of direction. The effect is real but modest, a nudge rather than a prison. The research has also produced surprises in the opposite direction. Speakers of languages that lack a future tense are sometimes said to save less, because the future feels less distinct from the present, but the finding is contested, and the effect, if it exists, is small. Speakers of languages with grammatical gender sometimes associate objects with masculine or feminine qualities, but the effect vanishes when the task does not involve language. These small, fragile effects are typical of the field: language nudges thought in the moment of speaking, but the nudge fades when the task changes. The picture that emerges is not of language as a prison or as a window but as a habit, one that shapes what is easy to notice without determining what can be thought. The sensible conclusion is that language is one influence among many on thought, and that the interesting question is not whether it influences thought but when, and how much.

The ban is therefore not a solution on its own. It is a question about what comes next, and a council that bans cars without providing an alternative has moved the problem, not solved it.

items.explanation: The daily ranges are Monday 15, Tuesday 10, Wednesday 16, Thursday 10 and Friday 11, so the week's average daily range is 62 / 5, which is 12.4 rupees. The bullish days are Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Monday's range of 15 and Wednesday's range of 16 are both above 12.4, while Friday's range of 11 is below it, so the count is 2. The threshold is not given in the question; it must be worked out from the table first, and counting the bullish days alone gives 3.
items.question: On how many days was the share bullish (Close above Open) AND the daily range (High - Low) greater than the week's average daily range?

items.explanation: With Wednesday's close free, the lowest possible closing price is Wednesday's Low of 99, which is below Tuesday's stated close of 100, so the lowest close in the week could have been 99, not 100. With Friday's close free, the highest possible closing price is Friday's High of 120. The largest possible difference is therefore 120 minus 99, which is 21. Using only the stated closes gives 18, and freeing Friday alone gives 20, since both miss that Wednesday's Low undercuts every stated close.
items.question: What is the largest possible difference between the highest and the lowest closing prices during the week, if the closing prices on Wednesday and Friday could each have been anywhere between that day's Low and High?

diagram.caption: Eight people in a row, facing north
diagram.content: A is at one of the ends. B sits immediately to the right of A. C is third from the left. D sits between B and F. E is at the right end. F sits immediately to the left of G. H is second from the right.

items.explanation: A is at the left end with B next to it, C is third and E is at the right end with H second from the right. F sits immediately left of G, and D sits between B and F, which forces the order A, B, C, D, F, G, H, E. The fourth person from the left is D.
options: F
D
G
H
items.question: Who sits fourth from the left?

items.explanation: The solved order from the left is A, B, C, D, F, G, H, E. After D and F swap, the order is A, B, C, F, D, G, H, E, so the person immediately to the left of G is D. Reading the original order gives F, which is the trap, and the swap must be applied before the neighbour is read.
options: D
F
H
E
items.question: If D and F swap places, who sits immediately to the left of G?

items.explanation: The solved order from the left is A, B, C, D, F, G, H, E. The fifth person from the left is F. The position cannot be found from any single clue; the whole row must be solved first.
options: F
G
D
H
items.question: Who sits fifth from the left?

items.explanation: The solved order is A, B, C, D, F, G, H, E. The person fourth from the left is D and the person second from the right is H. Between D and H sit F and G, which is 2 people. Both positions must be identified from the solved order before counting.
items.question: How many people sit between the person fourth from the left and the person second from the right?

items.explanation: The solved order from the left is A, B, C, D, F, G, H, E. Reversing it gives E, H, G, F, D, C, B, A, in which D is fifth from the left. The reversal moves every person, so D's new position is the mirror of its old one: 9 - 4 = 5.
items.question: If the row were reversed, so that everyone keeps their relative order but the left and right ends swap, what would the position of D be from the left?

items.explanation: Uttar Pradesh received 100 units. The given amounts there are Rice 35, Maize 25 and Pulses 10, leaving 30 units for Wheat and Barley together. Wheat in Uttar Pradesh is twice Barley there, so Barley in Uttar Pradesh is 10 units and Wheat is 20. Barley is therefore 10 in Punjab, 10 in Haryana, 10 in Uttar Pradesh and 10 in Bihar, a total of 40 units. The column total alone cannot give the Barley total; the Wheat-Barley relation in Uttar Pradesh must be solved first.
items.passage: Five foodgrains are distributed in four states. Each state received 100 units in total, and every amount is a multiple of 5 units. The amount of Wheat in Uttar Pradesh is twice the amount of Barley in Uttar Pradesh.
items.question: What is the total amount of Barley distributed across all four states, in units?

items.explanation: Maize is 20 units in Punjab, 15 in Haryana, 25 in Uttar Pradesh and 30 in Bihar, which add up to 90 units.
items.question: What is the total amount of Maize distributed across all four states, in units?

items.explanation: Let w, b and p be the Wheat, Barley and Pulses in Uttar Pradesh. Rice 35 and Maize 25 are known there, so w plus b plus p is 40. The standing order needs the Barley total, 30 plus b, to be at least 45, so b is at least 15. Since p is at least 5, w plus b is at most 35, and with w above b that gives twice b below 35, so b is at most 15. Hence b is exactly 15, w is above 15 and at most 20, so w is 20 and p is 5: the only feasible completion. The Wheat total is 25 plus 30 plus 20 plus 25, which is 100 units, so option A must be true. The Pulses total is 15 plus 20 plus 5 plus 15, which is 55, not 60, so option B fails; the Barley total is 30 plus 15, which is 45, not 50, so option C fails; and a Wheat total of 105 would need w equal to 25, which with b at least 15 leaves p at most 0, against positivity, so option D fails.
options: The Wheat total across all four states is 100 units.
The Pulses total across all four states is 60 units.
The Barley total across all four states is 50 units.
The Wheat total across all four states is 105 units.
items.question: Suppose the Wheat-Barley relation in Uttar Pradesh did not hold, and the Pulses figure for Uttar Pradesh was also unknown. The Wheat, Barley and Pulses amounts in Uttar Pradesh are each a positive multiple of 5 units. Wheat in Uttar Pradesh exceeds Barley in Uttar Pradesh, and a standing order requires the Barley total across all four states to be at least 45 units. Which of the following statements must be true?

items.explanation: Uttar Pradesh received 100 units. The given amounts are Rice 35, Maize 25 and Pulses 10, leaving 30 units for Wheat and Barley together. Wheat in Uttar Pradesh is twice Barley there, so Wheat is 20 and Barley is 10 units.
items.question: What is the amount of Wheat distributed in Uttar Pradesh, in units?

items.explanation: The Wheat amounts are Punjab 25, Haryana 30, Uttar Pradesh 20 and Bihar 25. After the change they are 25, 20, 20 and 35, so the highest is 35 and the lowest is 20, a difference of 15. The change moves the maximum and the minimum in opposite directions, so the range grows by more than the 10 units moved.
items.question: If the Wheat in Bihar were 10 units more and the Wheat in Haryana 10 units less, what would the difference between the highest and the lowest Wheat amounts across the four states then be, in units?

diagram.caption: Six startups and the funds they raised

items.explanation: Firm C existed from 2018 to 2022 and raised 13 crore in total, with 1 crore in 2018 and 1 crore in 2022, so its 2019, 2020 and 2021 amounts add up to 11 crore. Each amount is at most 5 in the middle year, and the only way to reach 11 is 3, 5 and 3, so C raised 5 crore in 2020.
items.passage: Six startups each raised funds over consecutive years. Each firm raised Rs 1 crore in its first and last year of existence. In any year, a firm's amount changed by at most Rs 2 crore from the previous year. All amounts are whole numbers of crores. The table gives each firm's first year, last year and total amount raised.
items.question: What is the amount raised by firm C in 2020, in Rs crore?

items.explanation: Take the largest possible 2021 amount for each firm and add them. A can reach 5, B can reach 4, C is fixed at 3, D can reach 3, E is fixed at 3 and F is in its first year at 1, giving a largest possible total of 19 crore.
items.question: What is the largest possible total amount raised by all six firms in 2021, in Rs crore?

items.explanation: Firm E existed from 2019 to 2022 and raised 8 crore in total, with 1 crore in 2019 and 1 crore in 2022, so its 2020 and 2021 amounts add up to 6 crore. Each amount is at most 3 crore, so both must be exactly 3 crore, and E raised 3 crore in 2020.
items.question: What is the amount raised by firm E in 2020, in Rs crore?

items.explanation: Take the smallest possible 2022 amount for each firm and add them. A cannot go below 2, B cannot go below 2, C is in its last year at 1, D cannot go below 2, E is in its last year at 1 and F cannot go below 2, giving a smallest possible total of 10 crore.
items.question: What is the smallest possible total amount raised by all six firms in 2022, in Rs crore?

items.explanation: Firm A existed from 2018 to 2023 and raised 16 crore in total, so its four middle years add up to 14 crore. Its 2021 amount is at most 5 crore, reached when the sequence is 1, 3, 3, 5, 3, 1, which respects the step limit of 2 crore per year and sums to 16. A larger 2021 amount would force the total above 16.
items.question: What is the largest possible amount raised by firm A in 2021, in Rs crore?

diagram.caption: Quarterly revenue of four products, 2024 (Rs lakh)

items.explanation: Product A's shares of the quarterly totals are Q1 40/105 = 38.1%, Q2 50/130 = 38.5%, Q3 45/140 = 32.1% and Q4 60/170 = 35.3%. The highest share is Q2, even though Product A's largest absolute revenue is in Q4. Absolute revenue and share give different answers, which is the point of the question.
items.question: In which quarter was Product A's revenue the highest as a share of that quarter's total revenue?

items.explanation: The quarterly totals are 105, 130, 140 and 170 lakh rupees. The increases are 23.8%, 7.7% and 21.4%, so the largest is 23.8%, which rounds to 24%. The largest absolute increase is in Q4, but as a percentage the Q1 to Q2 rise is larger.
items.question: What is the largest percentage increase in total quarterly revenue from one quarter to the next, in percent, rounded to the nearest whole number?

items.explanation: The first article ends at 200 into 0.80 into 1.25 = Rs 200, and the second ends at 200 into 1.25 into 0.80 = Rs 200. The two final prices are equal, so the first exceeds the second by Rs 0. The order of the two percentage changes does not matter, since multiplication commutes, which is the point the two articles are designed to test.
options: Rs 0
Rs 10
Rs 20
Rs 5
items.question: Two articles are each priced at Rs 200. The first is reduced by 20% and then increased by 25%. The second is increased by 25% and then reduced by 20%. By how many rupees does the first article's final price exceed the second article's final price?

items.explanation: From (a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab, 225 = 137 + 2ab, so ab = 44. Then a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)^3 - 3ab(a + b) = 3375 - 3 x 44 x 15 = 1395. Solving for a and b individually is unnecessary and the roots are not integers in general; the identity is the intended route, and cubing the sum without the correction term gives 3375.
items.question: Two distinct positive integers a and b satisfy a + b = 15 and a^2 + b^2 = 137. What is the value of a^3 + b^3?

items.explanation: Let the roots be 2t and 5t. Their product is 10 t^2 = 90, so t^2 = 9 and t = 3, giving roots 6 and 15. Then a^2 + b^2 = 36 + 225 = 261. The sum of the roots is 21, but squaring the sum alone counts 2ab twice, which is the trap in the largest distractor.
items.question: The roots of x^2 - Sx + 90 = 0 are positive integers in the ratio 2 : 5. What is the value of a^2 + b^2, where a and b are the roots?

items.explanation: From the first investment, P x 1.21 = 14,520, so P = Rs 12,000 and the interest earned is Rs 2,520. The second investment earns simple interest of 12,000 x 12 x 3 / 100 = Rs 4,320. The total interest is 2,520 + 4,320 = Rs 6,840.
items.question: A sum is invested at 10% per annum compound interest. After 2 years the amount is Rs 14,520. The same sum is then invested at 12% simple interest for 3 years. What is the total interest earned across both investments, in rupees?

items.explanation: Since log_4(x^2) = log_2(x^2) / log_2(4) = log_2 x, the condition is 2 log_2 x <= 26, so log_2 x <= 13 and x <= 8192. The largest perfect square not exceeding 8192 is 90^2 = 8100. A solver who converts only one logarithm, or who forgets the perfect-square condition and answers 8192, misses the final step.
items.question: What is the largest perfect square x such that log_2(x) + log_4(x^2) does not exceed 26?

items.explanation: Let AP = x and PB = 25 - x. For the foot of the altitude in a right triangle, CP squared equals AP times PB, so 144 = x(25 - x), giving x squared - 25x + 144 = 0, so x = 9 or 16. Then AC squared = AP times AB = 9 x 25 = 225, so AC = 15, and BC squared = 16 x 25 = 400, so BC = 20. The difference is 20 - 15 = 5 cm.
items.question: In triangle ABC, angle C is a right angle and the hypotenuse AB is 25 cm. The altitude from C meets AB at P, and CP is 12 cm. What is the difference between the lengths of AC and BC, in cm?

items.explanation: Meeting after 1 hour 30 minutes over 75 km gives Amit's speed plus Rohan's speed = 50 km/h. The time difference gives 75/v_Amit - 75/v_Rohan = 1 hour 15 minutes. Solving the two equations together gives Amit's speed 20 km/h and Rohan's 30 km/h. The meeting equation alone cannot fix either speed, and swapping who is slower gives 30 km/h, the trap option.
items.question: Towns A and B are 75 km apart, joined by a straight road. Amit travels from A to B while Rohan travels from B to A. They set off at the same time and pass each other after 1 hour 30 minutes. Amit gets to B 1 hour 15 minutes after Rohan gets to A. What is Amit's speed, in km per hour?

items.explanation: If the roots are integers a and b with a not equal to b, then a + b = 21 and k = ab. The possible pairs (a, b) with a < b are (1, 20), (2, 19), (3, 18), (4, 17), (5, 16), (6, 15), (7, 14), (8, 13), (9, 12), (10, 11), giving the distinct products 20, 38, 54, 68, 80, 90, 98, 104, 108, 110, so there are 10 possible values of k. Counting ordered pairs would double the answer, and allowing a = b would add one more value, both of which are the traps.
items.question: For how many integer values of k does the equation x^2 - 21x + k = 0 have two distinct integer roots?

items.explanation: Numbers leaving remainder 2 on division by 5 are 2, 7, 12, 17 and so on, and those that also leave remainder 3 on division by 7 form the sequence 17, 52, 87, 122, since the two conditions together repeat every 35. The smallest of them above 100 is 122: 122 leaves remainder 2 on division by 5 and remainder 3 on division by 7. The other options each satisfy one condition only: 112 and 117 fail the remainder on division by 7, and 127 fails the remainder on division by 5.
items.question: What is the smallest number greater than 100 that leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5 and remainder 3 when divided by 7?

items.explanation: Capital-months: A gives 12,000 x 4 + 18,000 x 4 + 12,000 x 4 = 168,000; B gives 18,000 x 4 + 12,000 x 8 = 168,000; C gives 24,000 x 4 + 30,000 x 8 = 336,000. The ratio is 1:1:2, so B receives one quarter of Rs 52,800, which is Rs 13,200.
items.question: A, B and C invest Rs 12,000, Rs 18,000 and Rs 24,000 in a business. After 4 months A adds Rs 6,000, B withdraws Rs 6,000 and C adds Rs 6,000. After 8 months A withdraws Rs 6,000. At the end of the year the profit is Rs 52,800. What is B's share, in rupees?

items.explanation: The tangent from P to the circle has length given by the square root of (17 squared minus 8 squared), which is 15 cm. By the power of a point, PA x PB equals the square of the tangent, so 9 x PB = 225 and PB = 25 cm. The result is consistent with the chord AB being 16 cm, the diameter, so this secant passes through the centre.
items.question: A point P lies 17 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 8 cm. A secant through P meets the circle at A and B, with A nearer P, and PA is 9 cm. What is the length PB, in cm?
items.stream_verdict: REBUILD: Single Pythagoras step gives the radius 12; the secant data is a redundant distractor that changes nothing.

items.explanation: The total age is 5 into 30 = 150 years. Removing the 10-year-old leaves 140 years across 4 members, an average of 35 years. That exceeds the average of all 5, which is 30 years, by 35 - 30 = 5 years. The average rises because the removed member was well below average, and the rise is the difference between the two averages, not the gap between the youngest and the average.
options: 35 years, by 5 years
35 years, by 10 years
32 years, by 2 years
30 years, by 0 years
items.question: The average age of 5 members of a family is 30 years. The youngest member is 10 years old. If the youngest is excluded, what is the average age of the remaining 4 members, and by how many years does it exceed the average age of all 5?

items.explanation: The sum is 9/2 x (10 + 8 x d) = 45 + 36 x d, where d is the common difference. Requiring 200 <= sum <= 400 leaves the sums 225, 261, 297, 333, 369, which is 5 distinct values. Counting every integer in the interval, instead of only those the sum formula can produce, overcounts the answer.
items.question: An arithmetic progression has 9 terms and first term 5. Its common difference is a positive integer and the sum of all its terms lies between 200 and 400 inclusive. How many distinct values can the sum of the progression take?

items.explanation: Of the 2000 people, 800 have the condition and 1200 do not. After the first test there are 600 true positives and 60 false positives. The second test keeps 480 of the true positives and 12 of the false positives, so among double positives the share who really have the condition is 480 / (480 + 12) = 40/41. Stopping after the first test, or quoting the second test's sensitivity alone, gives the wrong options.
items.question: In a population of 2000 people, 40% have a certain condition. A first test detects the condition in 75% of those who have it and wrongly reports it in 5% of those who do not. Everyone who tests positive on the first test takes a second, independent test, which detects the condition in 80% of those who have it and wrongly reports it in 20% of those who do not. What is the probability that a person who tests positive on both tests actually has the condition?

items.explanation: The scores total 35 x 42 = 1470. To push the lowest score as high as possible, the other 34 scores must be packed at the top of the range. With lowest score 25 a set of distinct scores totalling 1470 exists, while a lowest score of 26 forces even the smallest possible total above 1470, which is impossible. Hence the greatest possible lowest score is 25.
items.question: A class has 35 students whose scores are all distinct integers between 0 and 100 inclusive, and the class average is 42. What is the greatest possible score of the lowest-scoring student?

items.explanation: The powers of 4 modulo 11 cycle 4, 5, 9, 3, 1 with period 5, so the remainder 5 occurs exactly when n leaves remainder 2 on division by 5. The values of n up to 240 with that property are 2, 7, 12 and so on up to 237, which is (237 - 2) / 5 + 1, or 48 values. Checking only the first few powers misses most of them, and the other residue classes give different remainders.
items.question: How many integers n with 1 <= n <= 240 satisfy the condition that 4^n leaves remainder 5 when divided by 11?

items.explanation: The first inequality holds exactly for 1 < x < 12, which is 10 integers. The second requires |x| < sqrt(90), so x lies between -10 and 10. Intersecting the two ranges leaves 8 integers. Counting the first range alone, or forgetting that the second range cuts off the top end, gives the wrong options.
items.question: How many integers x satisfy both (x - 1)(x - 12) < 0 and x^2 < 90?

items.explanation: Let the quantities be 3k and 2k. After the first move they are 3k - 7 and 2k + 7, and the ratio 1 : 1 gives k = 14, so the quantities are 42 and 28, and after the move 35 and 35. Moving 5 units back gives 40 and 30, a ratio of 4 : 3. The second move does not simply undo the first, since only 5 units move back, so the original ratio of 3 : 2 is not restored.
items.question: Two quantities are in the ratio 3 : 2. If 7 units are moved from the first quantity to the second, the ratio becomes 1 : 1. If 5 more units are then moved from the second quantity back to the first, what is the ratio of the first quantity to the second?

items.explanation: Let the edges be m - d, m and m + d. Their sum is 3m = 24, so m = 8. The surface area is 2(lm + mn + nl) = 366, so l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 24^2 - 366 = 210. But l^2 + m^2 + n^2 is also 3m^2 + 2d^2 = 192 + 2d^2, giving d^2 = 9 and d = 3. The longest edge is m + d = 11 cm. The middle edge alone, or the sum of squares itself, would answer a different question.
items.question: A cuboid has edges in arithmetic progression. The sum of its three edges is 24 cm and its total surface area is 366 sq cm. What is the length of its longest edge, in cm?

items.explanation: A number is divisible by 4 exactly when its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. Counting the admissible last-two-digit pairs from {1, 2, 4, 5, 6} and filling the first two places from the remaining digits gives 36 numbers in total. Counting all permutations, or only checking the last digit, overcounts badly.
items.question: How many four-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, each digit used at most once, such that the number is divisible by 4?

items.explanation: Subtracting the two relations gives 4(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) - 4(2x - y + z) = -6, which completes to (2x - 2)^2 + (2y + 1)^2 + (2z - 1)^2 = 0, where each square matches its linear term. A sum of squares is zero only when each square is zero, so x = 1, y = -1/2 and z = 1/2, and then a = 4(1 + 1/4 + 1/4) = 6. Attempting to solve the two equations as a simultaneous system cannot work, since there are four unknowns and two equations.
items.question: Real numbers x, y and z, together with a number a, satisfy 4(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) = a and 4(2x - y + z) = a + 6. What is the value of a?

items.explanation: There are 27 outcomes in which the product is even, out of 36 in total. Of those, 3 have a sum greater than 10: (5, 6), (6, 5) and (6, 6). Only the first two have different numbers, so the conditional probability is 2/27. Counting (6, 6) as well gives 1/9, and dividing by 36 instead of by the 27 outcomes in the condition gives the other wrong options.
items.question: Two fair dice are thrown. Given that the product of the two numbers shown is even, what is the probability that their sum is greater than 10 and the two numbers are different?
